sections.title: Framing the endocrine history: screening symptoms

blocks.text: Endocrine disease is **protean**: many patients complain only of tiredness, weakness or lost drive. Because one hormone affects many organs, a short **systematic screen** of "hormonal" symptoms is part of every endocrine history, and screening questions about thyroid disease, diabetes and osteoporosis belong in any general assessment.

blocks.title: The endocrine symptom screen
items: **Weight and appetite**: always ask about both together (see table)
**Bowel habit**, **sweating** and **heat or cold intolerance**
**Thirst and urine volume** (polydipsia, polyuria, nocturia)
**Skin and hair**: pigmentation, bruising, thin or thick skin, acne, dryness, hair loss or excess
**Body size and shape**: height loss, change in ring, shoe, glove or hat size, coarsening features
**Reproductive**: menstrual pattern, galactorrhoea, libido, erectile function, subfertility or pregnancy loss
**Headache and vision**, and **lethargy or low mood**
**Development**: childhood growth, age at puberty and menarche, any disorder of sexual development

blocks.title: Appetite versus weight
rows: Cushing's syndrome; recurrent hypoglycaemia; hypothalamic disease

blocks.title: Non-specific presentations and their endocrine causes (Davidson)
rows: Hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, adrenal insufficiency, Cushing's, diabetes, hyperparathyroidism
Diabetes mellitus, adrenal insufficiency or thyrotoxicosis
Diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, hypercalcaemia of hyperparathyroidism, low potassium in Conn's
Phaeochromocytoma, a pituitary tumour or acromegaly
Cushing's, thyroid excess, hypokalaemia (e.g. Conn's), hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism

blocks.title: Bowel habit, sweating, pigmentation and height
items: **Diarrhoea**: hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency. **Constipation**: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause **either**
**Excess sweating**: hyperthyroidism, hypoglycaemia, acromegaly (and non-endocrine: anxiety, menopause)
**More pigmentation**: primary adrenal insufficiency, ACTH-driven Cushing's, acromegaly. **Less pigmentation**: hypopituitarism
**Height loss over 5 cm** suggests osteoporotic vertebral fractures

**Hair**: no facial hair in a man points to hypogonadism; temporal recession in a woman to androgen excess; loss of axillary and pubic hair in either sex to low adrenal androgens (hypogonadism, hypopituitarism, adrenal insufficiency)

blocks.title: Definitions worth knowing
rows: Diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus (central or nephrogenic), primary polydipsia (psychogenic or drug-related), hypercalcaemia, tubulointerstitial or cystic kidney disease
Turner's syndrome, hypothalamic or pituitary disease, imperforate hymen
Periods stopped for **6 months or more**
Pregnancy, menopause, PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, weight loss or anorexia
Hyperprolactinaemia (usually pituitary adenoma): in up to 80% of affected women and 30% of men

blocks.text: Lethargy can be hypothyroidism, Addison's or diabetes, but always think of **non-endocrine causes** too: anaemia, chronic infection (HIV, endocarditis), drugs, liver or kidney disease, occult cancer and depression.

Erectile dysfunction is **only occasionally endocrine** (primary hypogonadism, hyperprolactinaemia, hypopituitarism). Far more often it is vascular (endothelial disease), psychological or due to autonomic neuropathy from diabetes or alcohol.

blocks.title: What to ask for each disorder
rows: Heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss despite good appetite, palpitations at rest, tremor, irritability, loose stools, oligomenorrhoea, low libido
Eye complaints (grittiness, double vision, protrusion) point to **Graves'**, though stare and lid lag occur with any cause; ask about AF and heart failure symptoms
Cold intolerance, tiredness, weight gain, constipation, dry skin and hair, hoarse voice, poor memory, depression, myalgia, deafness
Insidious onset, so a **relative's account** is often revealing
Central weight gain, easy bruising, thin skin, acne, hirsutism, insomnia or psychiatric change, difficulty rising from a chair, back pain, menstrual change or ED, diabetes
Compare **old photographs**; ask about **steroid use** (the commonest cause)
Tiredness, anorexia, nausea, weight loss, diarrhoea, dizziness on standing, darker skin
ACTH deficiency (pituitary) mimics it but **without pigmentation**
Tighter rings, shoes, gloves or hats; coarser face; sweating; headache; failing vision; deeper voice; snoring or sleep apnoea; low libido or ED
**Sweating and headache** suggest the disease is still active
Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, weakness, weight loss, infections, pruritus vulvae or balanitis, lethargy
Hypoglycaemia instead gives morning headaches, sweating, seizures and weight gain

blocks.title: Pituitary disease: ask axis by axis, then about the mass
items: **ACTH** loss: lethargy, weight loss
**TSH** loss: cold intolerance, constipation
**Gonadotrophin** loss: low libido, ED, amenorrhoea, loss of secondary sexual hair
**GH** loss: reduced exercise capacity
**Mass effects**: headache (meninges), visual field loss (chiasm), diplopia (cavernous sinus: III, IV, VI), thirst, appetite or sleep change (hypothalamus), CSF rhinorrhoea (sphenoid sinus)

blocks.text: About **one-third** of people with acromegaly present because their appearance has changed and about **one-quarter** with headache or field loss; the rest are noticed in other clinics (GP, diabetes, hypertension, dental, dermatology).
In suspected hypothyroidism also ask about **other autoimmune disease**. In Cushing's, Talley flags **agitation and insomnia** as a red-flag symptom.

**Postpartum thyroiditis** can be mislabelled as postnatal depression, and **thyrotoxicosis** can masquerade as an anxiety disorder (palpitations, weight loss, diarrhoea). Screen with **TSH**; measure T4/T3 if TSH is abnormal.

sections.title: Past, drug, family and social history; emergencies

blocks.title: Past history clues
rows: Diabetes mellitus, sometimes first recognised after the birth

blocks.title: Drug history
rows: Hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis; more likely with pre-existing thyroid disease
Can precipitate thyrotoxicosis in a multinodular goitre
Past treatment of hyperthyroidism, a common route to hypothyroidism
Exogenous Cushing's; adrenal insufficiency if stopped abruptly after more than 3 weeks
Record replacement doses in hypopituitarism or hypoadrenalism

blocks.title: Family history
items: Thyroid disease, other **autoimmune** disease, diabetes, obesity, early cardiovascular disease
**MEN 1** (autosomal dominant): primary hyperparathyroidism (>90%), pituitary tumours (20%), GI tumours such as gastrinoma (70%)
**MEN 2**: think of it when relatives have medullary thyroid cancer or phaeochromocytoma

blocks.title: The diabetes history
items: Age at diagnosis, whether insulin was needed from the start, and how it presented
Current treatment (diet, metformin, sulphonylurea, GLP-1 analogue, insulin), understanding and adherence
Home glucose monitoring, HbA1c, **hypoglycaemic episodes** (a red flag) and past **ketoacidosis** admissions
Complications: eyes (laser or anti-VEGF treatment), nerves, feet, vessels, kidneys (urine protein, renal tests), erections
Coping at home and at work

blocks.title: Metabolic syndrome (Talley): 3 of 5 needed
rows: >130 systolic or >85 diastolic, or on treatment

blocks.text: Metabolic syndrome roughly **doubles** cardiovascular risk and gives about **five times** the risk of type 2 diabetes. Endocrine diseases are chronic, so the **social history** (coping at home and work) affects how well treatment works.

blocks.title: Endocrine emergencies to recognise from the history (Kumar)
rows: Collapse, postural hypotension, hypoglycaemia; chronic steroid use, or intercurrent illness, injury or surgery in Addison's
Sudden severe headache in a known or unrecognised pituitary tumour
Fever, tachycardia or fast AF, agitation, tremor
Bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, drowsiness or coma
Known type 1 diabetes, vomiting, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing
Type 2 diabetes, intercurrent illness, severe dehydration, drowsiness
Persisting polyuria despite dehydration; lithium or known DI

blocks.text: **Pituitary apoplexy** is easily mistaken for subarachnoid haemorrhage. Always ask about steroids, including ones **recently stopped**: abrupt withdrawal after more than 3 weeks can cause adrenal crisis.

sections.title: General endocrine examination: the head-to-toe screen

blocks.text: Endocrine examination is **mostly observation** and is tailored to the gland suggested by the history. In the first few seconds look for a **spot diagnosis**: acromegaly, Cushing's, Addison's, thyrotoxicosis, myxoedema, panhypopituitarism, virilisation or Paget's disease. Record **height, weight, BMI, blood pressure** and body habitus.

blocks.title: Screening sequence
rows: Large spade-like hands; sweaty palms, fine tremor, palmar erythema, onycholysis; carpal tunnel; pigmented creases; short metacarpals
Acromegaly; thyrotoxicosis; acromegaly or hypothyroidism; Addison's; pseudohypoparathyroidism
Hypertension; low BP or postural drop
Cushing's, Conn's, phaeochromocytoma, acromegaly; adrenal insufficiency
Hair loss; acanthosis nigricans, skin tags
Graves' eye signs; visual fields; optic atrophy; retinopathy
Coarse features, prognathism, large tongue; moon face, plethora; buccal pigmentation; candida
Goitre, nodules; hoarse or virilised voice
Thyroid disease; hypothyroidism or androgen excess
Pigmentation or pallor, vitiligo, striae, bruising, thin or thick, dry or greasy
Galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia; testicular volume (normal 15–25 mL), pubertal stage, virilisation

blocks.title: Visual fields by confrontation
items: Sit opposite the patient; each of you covers the **opposite** eye
Bring a **red pin** in slowly from the periphery; the patient says when it appears and if it disappears
Test **all four quadrants**, then repeat with the other eye
Typical pituitary defects: **upper temporal quadrantanopia** progressing to **bitemporal hemianopia** (macroadenoma pressing on the chiasm)
Formal perimetry is the standard test, but bedside confrontation with a red pin is sensitive

blocks.title: Signs of hypocalcaemia
items: **Trousseau's sign**: inflate a BP cuff above systolic pressure; carpal spasm appears within **2 minutes**
**Chvostek's sign**: tap the facial nerve just below the ear; the same side of the face twitches
Test both whenever there is a **thyroidectomy scar**

blocks.text: **Vitiligo** is a marker of autoimmunity: think of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Addison's disease and pernicious anaemia.

blocks.note: Look at: the head-to-toe examination map with photos of prognathism, spade hands, palmar crease pigmentation, vitiligo, multinodular goitre and pretibial myxoedema
Look at: the labelled whole-body diagram of endocrine signs (eyes, neck, hands, skin, hair, BP, breasts, genitalia)

sections.title: Thyroid examination: neck, thyroid status and eyes

blocks.title: Examining the neck
items: **Inspect** from the front and side: a goitre should be visible, with the line from cricoid to sternal notch bowing outwards
Give a **sip of water**: a goitre or thyroglossal cyst rises about 2 cm on swallowing; a **thyroglossal cyst also rises when the tongue is protruded**. Malignant fixation can stop the gland rising

**Palpate from behind**, neck slightly flexed, one lobe at a time: size, lower border (none felt suggests **retrosternal extension**), shape, nodules, consistency, tenderness, mobility, thrill. Repeat while swallowing
Then check **cervical nodes** and the **trachea** from the front, **percuss** the manubrium (unreliable) and **auscultate** each lobe for a bruit with the breath held
A thyroid bruit (hyperactive gland) must be told apart from a carotid bruit or a **venous hum**, which pressure at the base of the neck abolishes

blocks.title: Interpreting the gland
rows: Diffuse and tender (with fever, neck pain)
Subacute (de Quervain's) thyroiditis; also bleeding into a cyst
Carcinoma, calcified cyst or Riedel's thyroiditis

blocks.title: Numbers
items: Goitre affects about **10% of women and 2% of men**
Of people with a goitre, **80% are euthyroid**, 10% hypothyroid and 10% hyperthyroid
About **5% of palpable nodules** are malignant; suspect if hard, fixed, with nodes or vocal cord palsy, or larger than 4 cm
A goitre is found in **60–90%** of thyrotoxic patients

blocks.text: **Pemberton's sign**: the patient raises both arms beside the ears and holds them there for **a full minute**. Facial plethora, cyanosis, distended neck veins or inspiratory stridor mean a retrosternal goitre is obstructing the thoracic inlet. Students often fail by not waiting long enough.

blocks.title: Assessing thyroid status
rows: Slow, with slow, deep, croaky speech
Fine tremor, warm sweaty palms, palmar erythema, onycholysis
Cool dry skin, yellow palms (carotenaemia, sclerae spared), carpal tunnel
Sinus tachycardia or AF, sometimes collapsing
Periorbital puffiness, loss of outer eyebrows, xanthelasma, "peaches and cream" complexion
Hypothermia, non-pitting oedema, pericardial or pleural effusion, anaemia

blocks.text: **Lid retraction** (Dalrymple's sign) and **lid lag** (von Graefe's sign) come from sympathetic overactivity and occur in **any** thyrotoxicosis. **Exophthalmos, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, pretibial myxoedema and thyroid acropachy** are seen only in **Graves'**.

blocks.title: Examining Graves' eyes (Davidson)
items: Inspect from the front and side, and from **behind and above** the forehead: sclera visible below the iris means proptosis
Look for periorbital oedema, **chemosis** and corneal ulceration
Eye movements: **lid lag** on looking down, **diplopia** on lateral gaze (inferior rectus is often affected first)
Pupils: a **relative afferent pupillary defect**; vision: acuity, **colour vision**, fields
Fundi: disc pallor or papilloedema (optic nerve compression)
Orbitopathy is worse in smokers, can occur when euthyroid or hypothyroid, and radioiodine may worsen it

blocks.text: **Pretibial myxoedema** (raised, waxy, discoloured plaques over the shins from mucin deposition, driven by TSH-receptor antibodies) occurs **only in Graves'**, never in hypothyroidism. Brisk leg reflexes are present in only about 25% of thyrotoxic patients.

To show a **hung-up ankle jerk**, kneel the patient on a chair and tap the Achilles tendon: contraction is normal but **relaxation is delayed**. Myxoedema oedema is **non-pitting**, unlike the oedema of heart, kidney or liver failure.

blocks.note: Look at: onycholysis (Plummer's nails), the nail lifting off its bed in thyrotoxicosis
Look at: thyroid stare with exophthalmos (sclera visible around the iris)
Look at: myxoedema facies: puffy eyes, coarse dry skin, dull expression
Look at: drawings of proptosis with an afferent pupillary defect, lid retraction, and lid lag on downward gaze

blocks.text: Pituitary signs follow its **anatomy**: the optic chiasm lies above (bitemporal field loss), the sphenoid sinus below, and the **cavernous sinuses** laterally carry cranial nerves **III, IV, V and VI** (ocular palsies when a tumour extends sideways).

blocks.title: Hypopituitarism
items: Short stature (if childhood onset), **pallor**, fine wrinkled hairless "alabaster" skin, **no pigmentation**
A transfrontal scar from previous surgery
Visual fields and fundi (optic atrophy); cranial nerves III, IV, VI and V1
Reduced beard, axillary and pubic hair; **small firm testes** (normal adult volume 15–25 mL)
Talley gives the usual order of hormone loss as GH, prolactin, gonadotrophins, TSH, then ACTH; adenomas usually spare the posterior pituitary (loss of ADH causes diabetes insipidus)

blocks.title: Acromegaly
rows: Large spade-like hands, sweaty palms, tight rings, carpal tunnel syndrome
Frontal bossing (prominent supraorbital ridge), large nose, prognathism, widely spaced teeth, large tongue
Thick greasy skin, skin tags, acanthosis nigricans
Goitre, hypertension, cardiomegaly or heart failure, organomegaly, arthropathy, proximal myopathy

blocks.text: Signs of **active** acromegaly: many skin tags, heavy sweating, glycosuria, worsening field loss, an enlarging goitre, hypertension and headache. GH excess is diabetogenic in about **25%**, so check **urine glucose and BP**.

blocks.title: Examining for Cushing's
items: Stand the patient undressed: **moon face**, plethora, acne, hirsutism, **central obesity with thin limbs**, buffalo hump, supraclavicular fat pads
Skin: **thin**, easy bruising, wide **purple striae** (about 1 cm) on the abdomen; oedema
Spine: kyphosis and vertebral tenderness (osteoporotic fractures)
Ask the patient to squat or rise from a chair: **proximal myopathy**
Blood pressure, urine glucose and visual fields

blocks.text: Cause clues in Cushing's: **pigmentation, a short history, weight loss, oedema, hypokalaemia and marked weakness** favour **ectopic ACTH** (pigmentation also occurs in Nelson's syndrome); an **abdominal mass, virilisation or gynaecomastia in a man** suggests an **adrenal carcinoma**.

blocks.title: Addison's disease
items: Weight loss, wasting, dehydration
**Slate-grey-brown pigmentation** (in over 90%) of palmar creases and elbows, buccal mucosa and gums, genitals and **recent scars**: ACTH stimulates melanocytes
**Postural systolic drop** in 80–90%, even when lying BP is normal (mineralocorticoid deficiency)
Vitiligo, loss of body hair, and signs of other autoimmune gland failure

blocks.text: Secondary (pituitary) adrenal insufficiency causes **no pigmentation**, because ACTH is low rather than high. Common MCQ traps: moon face belongs to Cushing's, not acromegaly; Cushing's causes **hyperglycaemia**, while Addison's can cause **hypoglycaemia** and hyponatraemia.

blocks.title: The diabetic examination (Talley summary)
items: General: weight, hydration, pigmentation, **acetone on the breath**
Legs: necrobiosis, ulcers, infection, injection sites, foot temperature, **all peripheral pulses**, neuropathy
Eyes: cataract, retinopathy (fundoscopy), **third nerve palsy**
Mouth (candida), carotids, abdomen (injection sites, fatty liver)
Urinalysis (glucose, ketones, protein) and **lying and standing BP** (autonomic neuropathy)

blocks.note: Look at: the diagram of common acromegaly signs (frontal bossing, prognathism, large tongue, spade hands, field defect)
Look at: acromegaly photos showing an outgrown wedding ring, skin tags, a large tongue and prognathism
Look at: Cushing's syndrome with moon face and buffalo hump
Look at: wide purple abdominal striae in a man with Cushing's
Look at: pigmented palmar creases in Addison's disease

cards.front: Increased appetite with weight **loss**: which endocrine causes?
Reduced appetite with weight **loss**: which endocrine cause?
cards.back: Adrenal insufficiency (reduced appetite with weight gain suggests hypothyroidism)
Primary: no periods by 17 years. Secondary: periods stopped for 6 months or more

cards.front: How does ACTH deficiency from pituitary disease differ clinically from Addison's disease?
cards.back: Similar symptoms but **no excess pigmentation** (ACTH is low, not high)

cards.front: Which acromegaly symptoms suggest ongoing GH secretion?
Why does amiodarone disturb thyroid function?
cards.back: It is rich in iodine; it can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism, more so with prior thyroid disease
Primary hyperparathyroidism (>90%), pituitary tumours (20%), GI tumours e.g. gastrinoma (70%)

cards.front: Which steroid history risks adrenal crisis?
cards.back: Abrupt withdrawal of oral glucocorticoids taken for more than 3 weeks

cards.front: Endocrine causes of high and of low blood pressure?
cards.back: High: Cushing's, Conn's, phaeochromocytoma (also acromegaly). Low or postural drop: adrenal insufficiency
BP cuff inflated above systolic; carpal spasm within 2 minutes indicates hypocalcaemia

cards.front: Which thyroid signs are specific to Graves' disease?
cards.back: Exophthalmos, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia, pretibial myxoedema, thyroid acropachy (lid lag and retraction occur in any thyrotoxicosis)

cards.front: How is Pemberton's sign performed and what does it show?
cards.back: Arms raised beside the ears for a full minute; facial plethora, cyanosis, neck vein distension or stridor = retrosternal goitre obstructing the thoracic inlet

cards.front: Which neck lump rises on tongue protrusion as well as on swallowing?
Bedside sign with the highest LR+ for hypothyroidism?
Single best sign for Cushing's syndrome and the best sign against it?
cards.back: Thin skinfold (LR+ 29.7); absence of moon face (LR− 0.05)

cards.front: Where to look for pigmentation in Addison's disease?
cards.back: Palmar creases, elbows, buccal mucosa and gums, genitals, recent scars

cards.front: How common is postural hypotension in Addison's disease?
cards.back: In 80–90%, even when lying BP is normal

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman is eating more than ever but has lost 6 kg in three months. She opens her bowels four times a day and feels hot when colleagues are comfortable.
items.explanation: Big appetite with **weight loss**, frequent loose stools and **heat intolerance** make thyrotoxicosis the fit. Uncontrolled diabetes also gives hyperphagia with weight loss, but not heat intolerance or diarrhoea.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has little appetite yet has gained 5 kg. He is constipated, wears a jumper indoors in summer, and his wife says his voice has become husky.
items.explanation: Poor appetite with **weight gain**, constipation, cold intolerance and a hoarse voice point to hypothyroidism.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has four months of anorexia, nausea and loose stools and has lost 7 kg. She feels faint when she stands up quickly, and her skin has darkened even though it is winter.
items.explanation: Poor appetite with weight loss suggests adrenal insufficiency. **Darker skin** then places the problem in the adrenal gland itself: high ACTH stimulates melanocytes. Pituitary ACTH deficiency would cause pallor instead.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was diagnosed with acromegaly two years ago and had pituitary surgery. He attends clinic for review of whether his disease is controlled.
questions.leadIn: Which reported symptom most suggests continuing growth hormone excess?
options: Prognathism visible in photographs since diagnosis
Shoe size larger than ten years ago
A wedding ring that had to be cut off before surgery
questions.explanation: Sweating, headache and soft-tissue swelling reflect **ongoing GH secretion**. Bony and joint changes are permanent and do not show whether the disease is active now.
whyNot: Jaw growth is a permanent bony change and does not regress after cure.
A larger shoe size reflects past growth, not current activity.
Arthropathy is a lasting complication and does not track current GH levels.
This describes soft-tissue swelling before treatment, not now.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man had surgery and radiotherapy for a pituitary macroadenoma five years ago. He now has three months of tiredness, weight loss and dizziness on standing. He looks pale, with no skin darkening.
questions.leadIn: Deficiency of which hormone best explains these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Lethargy, weight loss and postural symptoms are those of **cortisol deficiency**. In pituitary disease ACTH is low, so the patient is **pale rather than pigmented**.
whyNot: TSH loss gives cold intolerance, constipation and weight gain rather than weight loss.
GH loss mainly reduces exercise capacity.
ADH loss presents with polyuria and thirst (diabetes insipidus).
Prolactin loss shows as failure of lactation after delivery.

questions.theme: Clues in the past, drug and family history
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with recurrent ventricular tachycardia has been on the same antiarrhythmic tablet for two years. He had a small goitre before starting it and now has weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance.
items.explanation: An iodine-rich antiarrhythmic, with **pre-existing thyroid disease**, causing hypothyroidism: amiodarone.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has had two kidney stones and a raised calcium. Her brother needed surgery for a gastrin-secreting tumour, and her father had a pituitary adenoma removed.
items.explanation: Hyperparathyroidism plus relatives with a **gastrinoma** and a **pituitary tumour**: the MEN 1 triad.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman with a long-standing nodular goitre had a CT pulmonary angiogram three weeks ago. She now has palpitations, a tremor and weight loss.
items.explanation: The iodine load of **contrast** can tip a multinodular goitre into thyrotoxicosis.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease last month. She reports tingling around her lips and cramps in her hands, and her wrist flexes when her blood pressure is taken.
items.explanation: Two steps: perioral tingling and carpal spasm with a BP cuff (**Trousseau's sign**) mean hypocalcaemia; after neck surgery, the cause is damage to the parathyroids.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has six months of headaches and keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. On confrontation testing with a red pin, she cannot see in the outer half of the field of either eye.
questions.leadIn: Where is the lesion most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Loss of both **temporal** fields means the crossing nasal fibres at the **chiasm** are damaged, classically by a pituitary macroadenoma growing upwards. The defect often starts in the upper temporal quadrants.
whyNot: An optic nerve lesion affects one eye only.
An optic tract lesion gives a homonymous (same-side) hemianopia.
An occipital lesion gives a homonymous defect, often sparing the macula.
Retinal disease does not produce a clean bitemporal pattern.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man has three months of tiredness and weight loss. His lying blood pressure is 104/70 mmHg and standing 82/60 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: Which further examination step best supports primary adrenal insufficiency?
options: Inspect the palmar creases and buccal mucosa for pigmentation
Look for lid lag on downward gaze
Inspect the shins for raised waxy plaques
Measure testicular volume with an orchidometer
questions.explanation: Postural hypotension plus weight loss suggests adrenal insufficiency; **pigmentation** of creases, mouth and scars (from high ACTH) confirms the problem is primary.
whyNot: Lid lag is a sign of thyrotoxicosis.
Pemberton's manoeuvre tests for a retrosternal goitre.
Pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease.
Testicular volume assesses hypogonadism and would not tell primary from secondary adrenal failure.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman developed fever, malaise and a painful neck radiating to her jaw a week after a viral illness. She is tremulous with a pulse of 112, and her gland is diffusely enlarged and very tender.
items.explanation: Thyrotoxic features plus **fever and a diffusely tender gland** after a viral illness: subacute thyroiditis.

items.stem: A 17-year-old boy has a smooth midline lump just below the hyoid. It moves up when he swallows and also when he sticks his tongue out.
items.explanation: Movement with **tongue protrusion** separates a thyroglossal cyst from a thyroid swelling.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a 5 cm stony hard nodule in the right lobe that does not move on swallowing. His voice is hoarse and there are enlarged nodes along the right jugular chain.
items.explanation: Hard, **fixed**, over 4 cm, with **nodes and a vocal cord palsy**: features of malignancy.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has a large nodular goitre whose lower edge cannot be felt. After holding her arms up beside her head for a minute, her face becomes congested and her neck veins swell.
items.explanation: Two steps: no palpable lower border suggests retrosternal extension, and a **positive Pemberton's sign** shows it obstructs the thoracic inlet.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman is referred with weight gain and possible Cushing's syndrome.
questions.leadIn: Which single examination finding most increases the probability of Cushing's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In Talley's good signs guide, a **thin skinfold** has an LR+ of about 30, far above any other sign.
whyNot: Generalised obesity (LR+ 0.12) actually makes Cushing's less likely.
Hypertension has an LR+ of only 1.5.
Striae have an LR+ of about 1.9.
Hirsutism has an LR+ of about 1.8.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old smoker has two months of rapidly worsening weakness, ankle swelling, hypertension and weight loss. His skin has darkened and his potassium is 2.8 mmol/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his Cushing's syndrome?
questions.explanation: A **short history, pigmentation, weight loss, oedema and hypokalaemia** favour ectopic ACTH, most often from a small cell lung cancer in a smoker.
whyNot: Pituitary Cushing's develops slowly and very high ACTH with pigmentation is unusual.
An adrenal adenoma suppresses ACTH, so there is no pigmentation.
Adrenal carcinoma suggests itself with an abdominal mass or virilisation, and ACTH is suppressed.
Exogenous steroids suppress ACTH and there is no drug history here.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a prominent brow, gaps between his lower teeth, thick greasy skin, many skin tags and glycosuria.
items.explanation: Frontal bossing, separated teeth, greasy skin and skin tags: acromegaly. Glycosuria and many skin tags suggest **active** disease.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man who had pituitary surgery is pale with fine, wrinkled, hairless skin. He shaves rarely, and his testes are small. There is no pigmentation.
items.explanation: Pallor, "alabaster" skin, loss of sexual hair and small testes after pituitary surgery: panhypopituitarism.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman speaks slowly, has puffy eyelids and yellowish palms with white sclerae. Her pulse is 54/min, and her ankle jerks relax slowly.
items.explanation: Carotenaemic palms (sclerae spared), bradycardia and **hung-up reflexes**: hypothyroidism.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years. Lying BP is 150/90 mmHg and standing 112/74 mmHg, his resting pulse is 100/min, ankle jerks are absent and he has no pigmentation.
items.explanation: Two steps: a postural drop without pigmentation or weight loss argues against Addison's; with long-standing diabetes and absent reflexes, it reflects **autonomic neuropathy**, the reason lying and standing BP is part of the diabetic exam.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has biochemically confirmed thyrotoxicosis and a goitre.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding indicates Graves' disease rather than another cause of thyrotoxicosis?
options: Raised waxy plaques over both shins
Fine tremor of the outstretched hands
questions.explanation: **Pretibial myxoedema** occurs only in Graves' disease. Lid lag, lid retraction, tremor and AF reflect thyroid hormone excess of any cause.
whyNot: Lid lag is due to sympathetic overactivity in any thyrotoxicosis.
Lid retraction is also sympathetic and non-specific.
Tremor occurs with thyrotoxicosis of any cause.
AF can complicate any thyrotoxicosis, especially in older patients.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man says he passes urine very often and wants to know if he has "polyuria".
questions.leadIn: Which finding defines true polyuria?
options: Urine output above 3 litres in 24 hours
Voiding more than 8 times a day
Waking twice or more at night to void
Urine output above 1.5 litres in 24 hours
questions.explanation: Polyuria is about **volume**: more than 3 L/day. Frequency alone may simply reflect small voided volumes.
whyNot: Frequency can occur with normal total volume (e.g. bladder irritation).
Nocturia is a symptom, not the definition.
1.5 L/day is a normal output.
Urgency suggests a bladder problem, not high volume.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has fatigue and weight gain. You examine her for hypothyroidism.
questions.leadIn: Which single sign has the highest positive likelihood ratio for hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: In Talley's good signs guide, **cool dry skin** has the highest LR+ (5.1), ahead of a pulse below 70 (3.9) and periorbital puffiness (3.2).
whyNot: Hypothyroid speech has an LR+ of about 2.3.
Goitre has an LR+ of about 2.6.
Coarse skin has an LR+ of about 2.6.
Periorbital puffiness has an LR+ of about 3.2, lower than cool dry skin.

questions.stem: You suspect a retrosternal goitre in a 70-year-old woman and plan to test for Pemberton's sign.
questions.leadIn: Which describes the correct technique?
options: Arms raised beside the head and held for about a minute before judging
Arms raised briefly and lowered at once
Patient lies flat and coughs while you watch the neck
Neck hyperextended while you palpate from behind
Patient sips water with the arms by the sides
questions.explanation: The arms must stay up for **a full minute**; only then may facial plethora, cyanosis, neck vein distension or stridor appear. Not waiting is a common reason students fail this step.
whyNot: A brief raise misses the sign, which takes time to develop.
Coughing lying flat is not part of the test.
Palpation from behind assesses the gland, not inlet obstruction.
Swallowing water tests whether a lump moves with the thyroid.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman has gained 8 kg over a year. She is hungry all the time, wakes with headaches, and has episodes of sweating and shakiness that settle when she eats.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Step 1: pair appetite with weight. **Increased appetite with weight gain** narrows the field to Cushing's, hypoglycaemia or hypothalamic disease. Step 2: look for the discriminator. **Morning headaches and sweating episodes relieved by food** are the history of hypoglycaemia, and repeated eating drives the weight gain.
whyNot: Hypothyroidism gives weight gain with a **poor** appetite and no sweating attacks.
Thyrotoxicosis gives sweating with a big appetite, but weight **falls**.
Adrenal insufficiency gives a poor appetite and weight loss.
Diabetes insipidus presents with polyuria and thirst, not hunger.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man who smokes has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years and hypertension. He has gradually developed erectile dysfunction. His libido is normal, and he has normal facial and body hair and normal-sized testes.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely mechanism of his erectile dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Step 1: remember that ED is **only occasionally endocrine**. Step 2: look for endocrine clues. Normal libido, normal sexual hair and normal testes argue against low testosterone. Step 3: weigh the risk factors. Smoking, diabetes and hypertension point to **vascular** disease (autonomic neuropathy is the other common diabetic cause).
whyNot: Hyperprolactinaemia usually lowers libido and may cause galactorrhoea.
Primary hypogonadism gives low libido, reduced sexual hair and small testes.
Hypopituitarism causes loss of sexual hair, pallor and other axis failures.
Hypothyroidism is not a usual cause of isolated ED.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is seen three months after giving birth. She feels tired and low and was told she has postnatal depression. Her mother mentions she has become very slow and puts on extra layers indoors.
questions.leadIn: Which condition is most important to exclude?
questions.explanation: Step 1: the onset is insidious, so the **relative's account** (slowness, cold intolerance) adds signs of hypothyroidism. Step 2: the setting is postpartum. Step 3: postpartum thyroiditis is often **mislabelled as postnatal depression**, so check TSH.
whyNot: Cushing's gives central weight gain, bruising and striae, not cold intolerance.
Acromegaly develops over years with coarse features and growing hands.
Phaeochromocytoma gives paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitations.
Hyperparathyroidism gives thirst, stones and constipation rather than cold intolerance.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has not had a period for 8 months. A pregnancy test is negative, and she has noticed milky fluid from both nipples.
items.explanation: Secondary amenorrhoea (6 months or more) with **galactorrhoea**: hyperprolactinaemia, usually a pituitary adenoma.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man has attacks of pounding headache, drenching sweats, palpitations and pallor. His BP during an attack is 210/120 mmHg.
items.explanation: Paroxysms of headache, sweating and palpitation with **severe episodic hypertension**: phaeochromocytoma.

items.stem: A 53-year-old woman is thirsty, passes large volumes of urine, is constipated and low in mood, and has had renal colic. Her fasting glucose is normal.
items.explanation: Two steps: thirst, polyuria, constipation, stones and low mood suggest **hypercalcaemia**; the endocrine cause to think of is primary hyperparathyroidism.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man has hypertension despite three drugs, proximal muscle weakness and polyuria. His potassium is 2.9 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Resistant hypertension with **hypokalaemia** causing weakness and polyuria: Conn's syndrome.

questions.theme: What a thyroid examination sign means
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with a toxic multinodular goitre follows your finger downwards; a rim of white sclera appears above the iris as the lid trails behind.
items.explanation: Lid lag in a patient **without Graves'** shows it is sympathetic, not infiltrative.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with Graves' eye disease reports that colours look washed out in her right eye. When a light is swung to that eye, both pupils dilate.
items.explanation: Reduced **colour vision** and a **relative afferent pupillary defect** mean the swollen orbit is compressing the optic nerve.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a diffuse goitre has a soft systolic sound over both lobes. It persists when you press at the base of the neck, and her carotids are quiet.
items.explanation: Not abolished by pressure (so not a venous hum) and not carotid: a **thyroid bruit**, from increased blood flow in an overactive gland (Graves').

items.stem: Two days after thyroid surgery, tapping just below a woman's ear makes the corner of her mouth twitch on that side.
items.explanation: **Chvostek's sign**: hypocalcaemia, here from parathyroid damage at surgery.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation.
questions.leadIn: Which examination finding best supports hypothyroidism?
options: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands
questions.explanation: **Bradycardia** (a pulse below 70 has an LR+ of about 3.9) fits hypothyroidism. The other options are thyrotoxic signs.
whyNot: Fine tremor is a thyrotoxic sign.
Warm sweaty palms are thyrotoxic; hypothyroid skin is cool and dry.
Hypothyroid reflexes are slow to relax, not brisk.
Onycholysis (Plummer's nails) occurs in thyrotoxicosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo has needed much less insulin recently because of frequent hypoglycaemia. She is tired and has lost weight. Her BP falls on standing, and her buccal mucosa shows brown patches.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune background (type 1 diabetes, vitiligo), hypoglycaemia, weight loss, postural hypotension and **buccal pigmentation** point to Addison's disease.
whyNot: Pituitary ACTH deficiency does not cause pigmentation.
Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, not pigmentation or postural hypotension.
Thyrotoxicosis can raise insulin needs but does not pigment the mouth.
Cushing's causes hyperglycaemia and hypertension.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has a phaeochromocytoma removed. His mother had a medullary thyroid carcinoma.
questions.leadIn: Which inherited syndrome is most likely?
options: Sporadic phaeochromocytoma with no inherited cause
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid cancer plus phaeochromocytoma in a family should make you think of **MEN 2**.
whyNot: MEN 1 links hyperparathyroidism, pituitary and GI tumours.
Autoimmune polyglandular syndromes cause gland failure, not tumours.
This would not explain phaeochromocytoma or medullary cancer.
A family history of medullary thyroid cancer makes a sporadic tumour unlikely.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the best match from the list. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman is found drowsy at home in winter. Temperature 34.6°C, pulse 46/min, BP 90/60 mmHg. Her face is puffy, her legs have non-pitting swelling, and her daughter says she stopped her "thyroid tablets" months ago.
items.explanation: Hypothermia, bradycardia, drowsiness and non-pitting oedema after stopping thyroxine: myxoedema coma.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden, devastating headache and double vision. His BP is 88/56 mmHg.
items.explanation: Two steps: a sudden "thunderclap" headache could be subarachnoid haemorrhage, but a **known pituitary tumour**, ocular palsy (cavernous sinus) and hypotension (acute ACTH loss) make it apoplexy.

items.stem: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomited for two days. She is dry and is taking deep, sighing breaths.
items.explanation: Known type 1 diabetes, vomiting, dehydration and **Kussmaul breathing**: DKA.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has taken prednisolone for polymyalgia for 8 months. He stopped it suddenly when he was admitted with pneumonia, and now collapses. BP 74/40 mmHg, glucose 2.6 mmol/L.
items.explanation: Abrupt withdrawal of long-term steroids during an intercurrent illness, with collapse, hypotension and hypoglycaemia: adrenal crisis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has noticed her scalp hair receding at the temples over a year. Her voice has deepened and she now shaves her chin.
questions.leadIn: Which hormonal disturbance does this history suggest?
questions.explanation: **Temporal recession** in a woman, with a deeper voice and facial hair, means androgen excess (virilisation).
whyNot: Hypothyroidism causes dry, coarse hair and loss of the outer eyebrows, not virilisation.
Hypopituitarism causes loss of body hair.
Adrenal insufficiency reduces adrenal androgens and causes loss of axillary and pubic hair.
Hyperprolactinaemia presents with amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a waist of 108 cm and BP of 138/88 mmHg. Fasting triglycerides 2.1 mmol/L, HDL 1.2 mmol/L, fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L. He takes no regular medication.
questions.leadIn: Using the criteria in Talley, does he have the metabolic syndrome?
options: No: only 2 of 5 criteria are met
No: a fasting glucose above 5.6 mmol/L is essential
questions.explanation: BP (>130/>85), waist (>102 cm) and triglycerides (>1.7) qualify; HDL 1.2 is above the male cut-off of 1.0, and glucose is below 5.6. **Three of five** is enough.
whyNot: HDL and glucose are both normal, so only three are met.
BP, waist and triglycerides are all abnormal.
No single criterion is mandatory; any 3 of 5 qualify.
HDL and glucose are within the thresholds.

ospe.identify: Endocrine spot signs: prognathism and spade hands (acromegaly), palmar crease pigmentation (Addison's), vitiligo, multinodular goitre, pretibial myxoedema (Graves')
Onycholysis (Plummer's nails): separation of the nail from its bed in thyrotoxicosis
Thyroid stare with exophthalmos: sclera visible around the iris, a Graves' sign
Myxoedema facies: puffy eyelids, coarse dry skin and a dull, slow expression (hypothyroidism)
Acromegaly: outgrown wedding ring, skin tags, macroglossia and prognathism
Cushing's syndrome: moon face and buffalo hump
Palmar crease pigmentation: primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)
Vitiligo of the fingers: autoimmune marker (Hashimoto's, Addison's, pernicious anaemia)
